prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical discovery of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators and for the experimental observation of the quantum spin Hall state in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: Topological insulators are a new class of matter defined by topology rather than by broken symmetry, and the evidence is of the kind this committee can trust. The HgTe quantum-well transport measurement showed quantized edge conductance of 2e^2/h in small devices, with the dependence on gate voltage and device size expected from theory, and later spectroscopy and transport on other materials agreed. The chain from theory (Kane and Mele's Z2 classification and quantum spin Hall proposal) to the original experiment (Molenkamp's group) is traceable and the experiment was decisive. The field has been stable and independently confirmed for about fifteen years, and it has changed how materials, spintronics and quantum-device communities think about protected states. Recognition is mature and, if anything, overdue. On reflection I now favour the Kane, Mele and Molenkamp configuration over my opening trio, because it keeps the two originators of the theory together with the original experiment on the effect itself.
statement.case_against: The credit is genuinely messy. The Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal that told Molenkamp which material to use is outside the supplied names, and one of its authors is deceased, so a three-person prize leaves out a decisive step. Hasan's group did the first spectroscopy of three-dimensional topological insulators (Bi-Sb, Bi2Se3), and a trio of Kane, Mele and Molenkamp omits that original experiment even though it is arguably as important for materials as the 2D result. Other ARPES groups and the Fu-Kane-Mele and Moore-Balents theory also bear on priority. A citation that is fair to the 2D story is therefore not fair to the 3D story, and the committee must accept that limitation or choose differently. The quantum anomalous Hall candidate is a closely related discovery that would not be recognised.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 insulators first as a universal mechanism, proposes Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, and asks whether the prize should split the two-dimensional and three-dimensional parts of the story, noting that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang are outside the credit.
responses.response: I agree with the physics and with your trio, and your argument has moved me on Mele. In my opening I left him out for Hasan, but I said then that omitting him was hard to justify, and I accept that. Kane and Mele are co-originators, and the original experiment on the effect they predicted is Molenkamp's. I do not agree that Hasan's work is merely an add-on. It was the first observation of a protected surface state on a three-dimensional material, which for those of us who work with real samples is where the field became a materials discovery. I would keep that as the principal reservation, and I would like the committee to look at the historical record on Bi-Sb before it is set aside. Where we agree is that the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal cannot be solved by adding names, so the citation should be worded around the observation and the classification, not around a claim of first prediction of the HgTe system.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks IceCube's high-energy astrophysical neutrinos first, as a detector-driven discovery that opened a new window, mature and confirmed in several channels, with the Halzen-Karle split not fully settled.
responses.response: This is a strong candidate, and a new window onto the universe is the kind of door I like. My reservation is the one you partly raise yourself. The discovery is a collaboration result, and I am not yet sure that the original contribution is correctly carried by two people. Halzen's concept and leadership are clear, but Karle's decisive role versus that of the analysts who found the diffuse flux, and the earlier AMANDA programme, are exactly where I would want the historical record before I am absolutely sure. The source identification is also mostly from one experiment. I keep B016 as an alternative, not as my first choice, and would move toward it if the attribution can be documented more firmly than the supplied text allows.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, ranks IceCube first and the optical lattice clock second, valuing detector-driven discoveries with careful calibration, and states that he relies on colleagues for credit details outside his own field.
responses.response: I share your preference for instrument-driven discoveries and agree that the lattice clock is a clean invention with a clean two-person attribution, which is why it is my main alternative. Since you defer to us on the condensed-matter credits, I should say plainly that the HgTe result is the more original experiment in that it showed a phenomenon that had not been seen before, while the lattice clock performs an existing kind of measurement much better and builds on the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize. That distinction between a new observation and an improvement matters to me under the discovery criterion, and I would not treat the redefinition of the second as a requirement for waiting.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first, as a prediction by Bistritzer and MacDonald followed by the Jarillo-Herrero observation, and notes the open question of earlier moire theory.
responses.response: I ranked this seventh, and I take your enthusiasm seriously, since the prediction-then-experiment narrative is attractive and many groups have reproduced the correlated phases. The reason I hold back is that the origin of the superconductivity is still unresolved and sample dependence is large, so I cannot yet be absolutely sure of what has been discovered. There is also an attribution problem on the experimental side, since the lead student and other early groups are not in the credit. Topological insulators have had fifteen years to settle, and this field has had about eight, and I would prefer the committee wait for that difference to narrow.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first as a clean, widely reproduced demonstration of quantum optics on a chip, while flagging the overlap with the 2025 prize and a possible conflict of interest in his own field.
responses.response: I appreciate that you flagged your own closeness to the field. On substance, I find the 2004 strong-coupling experiment convincing and mature, but I think the timing after the 2025 circuits prize is a real obstacle, and the attribution among Blais, Girvin, Huang, Schoelkopf and Wallraff is not clean in three names. I ranked it outside my top eight for that reason. I would not exclude it for all time, but I would put it behind candidates that have no recent prize in the same hardware.

uncertainties: Whether the historical record supports crediting Hasan's 3D ARPES discovery as an original discovery on a par with the HgTe experiment, and whether it can be accommodated within three people.
How to word the citation fairly given that the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal and the later 3D theory (Fu, Kane, Mele; Moore, Balents) fall outside the three names.
Whether the quantum anomalous Hall effect should be considered together with, or after, this prize.
Priority and independence of other early ARPES and transport groups, which I cannot check from the supplied text.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for any shortlisted candidate: I have no documented collaboration with the credited people. My colleague Goran Johansson is also at Chalmers Physics and is close to the circuit QED community, but that concerns B026 and not my preferred configuration, and I have no personal tie to it.
